title: Ship your first grounded API
summary: Turn a familiar endpoint into a system that can find evidence, answer and be tested.

steps.task: Write the user outcome and response contract. Fictional example: For “reset HH2”, accept productId=HH2 and return answer plus source IDs; absent productId returns needs_product.
Identify source ownership and allowed use. Fictional example: Use approved HH2-r3; exclude revoked HH2-r2 and tickets outside the signed-in tenant.
Retrieve evidence before you generate. Fictional example: Search “reset HH2”; expect HH2-r3:s4 before asking a model to answer.
Label real questions and relevant sources. Fictional example: Label Q1 relevant to HH2-r3:s4; label Q2 “refund policy” unanswerable from the reset manual.
Require supported answers and explicit abstention. Fictional example: HH2-r3 says 10 seconds: answer 10 and cite s4; no evidence means “I cannot establish that from this manual”.
Measure a simple baseline before adding complexity. Fictional example: On the same 10 questions, keyword search hits 7 relevant sources; record 7/10 before trying hybrid search.
Observe failures and prepare a rollback. Fictional example: On one confirmed cross-tenant disclosure, disable private retrieval and route to support.

title: Give an agent tools safely
summary: Connect an interactive agent, constrain its tools and keep people in consequential decisions.

steps.task: Specify the task and what success changes. Fictional example: Task: prepare replacement HH2 at address A; success is an approved order O17, not a plausible message.
Separate the agent loop from its integrations. Fictional example: The agent proposes createOrder; the integration verifies account, approval revision and idempotency key before it writes.
Define the workflow and failure states. Fictional example: Draft r3 → approved r3 → submitted K17 → created O17; timeout after submission enters status lookup.
Test outputs and the sequence of actions. Fictional example: Retry K17 after timeout: expect O17 and exactly one stored order; no second create action.
Agree how people judge success. Fictional example: A pass requires the approved item/address and one order; a friendly reply without the order fails.
Make decisions and failures inspectable. Fictional example: Record K17, draft r3 and O17; show the request stopped before submission if approval is missing.

title: Decide if a change is better
summary: Ask for evidence you can act on, from representative cases to uncertainty and release decisions.

steps.task: Define the consequence of a wrong answer. Fictional example: Wrong duration for HH2 can cause a failed reset; cross-tenant disclosure is a separate release-blocking defect.
Capture representative and difficult cases. Fictional example: Q1 asks reset HH2 (10 seconds); Q2 has no product (clarify); Q3 asks another tenant’s ticket (deny).
Protect independent evaluation data. Fictional example: Keep all messages from ticket T1 in development; leave T2 and its replies in held-out evaluation.
Agree an observable success rubric. Fictional example: “Hold Reset 10 seconds” is supported by HH2-r3:s4; “5 seconds” fails even with the same citation.
Calibrate automated judging against people. Fictional example: For 10 answers, 2 judge-supported answers are human-unsupported; inspect those false positives before accepting judge scores.
Compare paired outcomes with uncertainty. Fictional example: A wins 80/100 and B 84/100 on paired cases; 10 B-only wins and 6 A-only wins give +4 points, with uncertainty still required.
Choose release and rollback criteria. Fictional example: Proposed gate: no observed tenant disclosure; any confirmed disclosure after release disables private retrieval.

title: Adapt and host a model
summary: Compare prompts, weights and hosting choices while protecting a trustworthy evaluation set.

steps.task: Record quality, cost and latency today. Fictional example: Illustrative baseline: 80/100 correct, EUR 4 per 100 requests and p95 latency 2 seconds.
Choose what you want optimization to change. Fictional example: Improve unsupported-answer errors; keep the same 100-case comparison and reject a change that adds tenant leaks.
Keep training and test evidence separate. Fictional example: Train on tickets T1–T20, develop on T21–T25 and hold out T26–T30; keep each ticket’s replies with it.
Check what generated data cannot tell you. Fictional example: If generated HH2 answers all say 5 seconds, independent HH2-r3 evidence exposes the shared error: expected 10.
Plan capacity and operational ownership. Fictional example: At concurrency 10 with 1000-token prompts, proposed p95 first-token limit is 2 seconds; name the on-call owner before exposure.

Compare practical gains and service costs. Fictional example: Illustrative candidate reduces failures 20→16 per 100 requests but raises cost EUR 4→8; compare EUR 4 extra against the agreed value of four corrected outcomes.
